To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
thermionic converters are superior to thermoelectric converters for high temperature applications (above 800degK).

thermoelectric generators are not a viable option for power generation from waste heat at low temperature (below 400degK), while thermionic converters are an option for high temperatures (above 800degK) with the potential to reach Carnot efficiency.

(i) the thermionic efficiency at high temperatures is higher than that of thermoelectrics and (ii) the thermoelectric efficiency at low temperatures is higher than thermionics, but only if the workfunction of the electrodes is low enough.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of thermoelectric and thermoionic microgenerators.

(a) thermoelectric and (b) thermionic energy conversion and cooling, (c) thermoelectric generators (TEG) and thermionic generators (TIG) for power generation and (d) thermoelectric refrigeration (THER) and thermionic refrigeration (THIR) for cooling applications.
the development of thermionic and thermoelectric micro- and nanostructured devices for power generation and refrigeration.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
thermoelectric devices are the only choice for low temperatures (below 400degK), while thermionic devices are to be preferred at high temperatures (above 800degK).
the thermionic converter, as a power generator, has a great potential for future applications.
thermoelectric generators are the only realistic option for low temperature (T < 400degK), low efficiency applications.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the thermionic converter is the most promising microgenerator for high temperatures and the thermoelectric generator for low temperatures, whereas the thermoelectric microgenerator is the only candidate for intermediate temperatures (400-800degK).
the thermionic converter is a promising device with a high potential for power generation and refrigeration applications.
thermoelectric generators are the most promising devices for micro- and nanoscale power generation, while for large scale power generation and cooling, thermionic converters are more promising.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the efficiency of a thermionic converter is determined by the work function difference between both electrodes.
the thermoelectric effect is not a fundamental effect but rather a result of the bandstructure and the scattering processes.
the thermionic converter is an efficient and promising technology for the conversion of thermal energy to electricity, which is especially interesting in the case of high-temperature waste heat.
